Richmond, Va., May 9.

Governor Davis has issued an invitation to the local officers charged with law enforcement in the camp communities to meet with him and leading State and Federal officials at Richmond on May 9th to consider ways and means of better protecting the health and morals of our soldier and sailor heroes now in training in Virginia. More than two hundred officials have been invited to attend, including the ranking army and navy officers stationed in this State. The importance of this conference is emphasized by the Governor in his letter to those he has asked to attend the conference.

"In order" Governor Davis says, "to protect the health and morals of our soldiers, sailors and marines, and of the munitions, shipyard and other war workers, as well as of the civil population, the War and Navy departments have requested the governors of the several States to cooperate in law enforcement in the communities contiguous to military and naval camps and in which are located large war industrial establishments.

Realizing that closer cooperation between these communities in Virginia, and between our State and local officials with the Federal government, is essential to more successful law enforcement, I deem it advisable that a meeting be held immediately to consider this problem. I have, therefore, called a meeting of all officers charged with law enforcement in the camp communities of Virginia, health officers, and others interested in this phase of war service to meet at Richmond on Thursday, May 9, 1918, at 10 A.M. in the Hall of the House of Delegates."

The Governor stated today that he hoped every official invited would attend this conference, and it was in the interest of patriotic service that Virginia should make every effort properly to perform.

An otherwise dull and quiet meeting frightened up little last night by Alderman Powers, who, in speaking to a resolution calling upon the city auditor to produce a report as to ways and means by which the city might meet its obligations without increasing taxation, intimated that some one in opposing such a motion apparently inclined toward the process of "whitewashing."

Alderman Mitchell was the only member who expressed himself against such motion, as being unnecessary at this time, unless the heads of the departments be joined with the auditor; that gentleman took exception to what had been intimated by Alderman Powers.

The resolution offered by Mr. Powers calls upon the auditor to present the council a report as to what, in his opinion, could be done in the shape of eliminating expenses, and as to how the government can be conducted.

The following account of the killing in action of Capt. B. T. DIXON, taken from letter OF Lieut. Wright T. Dixon, machine gun COMPANY, 120th Inft, 30th division, twin brother of Captain Dixon, to his brother, S. J. Durham, of Gastonia:

With the British Army in France, April 28.—By the Associated Press General Von Arnim, Commander of the German troops in the Ypres sector, paused last night in his drive against the entente allied territory about KENNEL, undoubtedly to enable his forces to make a fresh attack.


(By Associated Press)


The loss of Mont KENNEL has evidently failed to disorganize in any way the allied resistance in the Ypres region. The line in fact, seems to have stiffened since this isolated height was taken by the Germans, and the enemy, after a day of desperate struggling yesterday, found himself held fast everywhere.


Hun Attacks Futile.
Locre, west of Mont KENNEL, and Voormezeele, two miles south of Ypres, were the chief points under attack by the Germans in their vain effort to develop their success of the previous day. At each, although the fighting fluctuated during the day, the enemy failed to gain his objectives and today is no further advanced toward them than he was yesterday morning.
The French fought with great gallantry in the Locre sector, inflicting severe losses on the enemy in his four attacks, the last of which carried him into the village. Last evening the French counterattacked vigorously and regained the place.


Hundreds Were Taken.
The British were no less stubborn in their defense of Voormezeele at which points they were obliged to hold fast; the line curving to the east and north around Ypres was not to be abandoned. To-day found them still in possession of the village and holding fast in the wood on the ridge southwest of the town. Several hundred prisoners were taken by the British in this fighting.


Will Abandon Ypres.
There seems a quite general disposition on the part of military observers to forecast the eventual abandonment of the Ypres salient as the result of the fall of Mont KENNEL. It has been pointed out by the British War Office that this result will not necessarily follow. It is likewise observed, however, that should an evacuation of Ypres become necessary, the taking of Mont KENNEL has not destroyed the defensive value of the range of hills to the west from which it stood out, and which have been referred to as the backbone of the Flanders position. At no time in the history Of our
country has the menace Of fire been
greater and the preservation OF our
resources more necessary. ActlVl-
ties of hostile incendiaries threaten
in many parts of the country, caus-
ing destruction of needed supplies
of foodstugs and other vital staples.
These fires will strike at the foun-
dation of national power and wealth
by the elimination of resources.


Fire causes enormous direct de-
struction of cotton, lumber, grain
and other foodstuffs, as well as a
large variety of other materials es-
sential to the prosecution Of the
war. Fire cripples productive in
dustry engaged upon war orders to
a far greater extent than is gener-
ally realized.


While causing a vast impairment
in Americas fighting efficiency, fire
loss is, in the main, unnecessary.
The loss can be materially lessened
if each citizen will do his part to-
wards seeing that precautionary
measures are adopted for his premis-
es. The burning of your property
through negligence or carelessness
may not only cause loss and incon-
venience, but the fire may spread to
your neighbor's property also. Fire
prevention, therefore, becomes pa
triotic duty of every citizen. The
cooperation of newspapers, civic
bodies, and particularly school sys-
TENS, will contribute powerfully to
this end. The annual loss by fire to
the state of South Carolina is ap-

dred and Fifty Thousand Dollars.

our citizens to the magnitude of the
fire waste and induce them to take
more interest in the subject of fire
prevention, I, Richard I. Manning,
Governor of the State, by virtue of

designate and proclaim Saturday,
November 2, 1918, as Fire Proven

removal therefrom of all rubbish
and debris; that chimneys, flues and
heating apparatus be put in order;
that the mayor of each town and
city by proclamation ask the cooper
alton of it's citizens in having a thor
ough inspection of all premises in
their respective municipalities, to
the end that the number of fires
may be lessened and the losses there
from checked.

unto set my hand and caused


the great seal of the State of
South Carolina to be affixed at
Columbia on this the twenty


third day of October, in the


year of our Lord nineteen hun
dred and eighteen.


Richard I. Manning,


Governor.

Secretary of State.

DEAR MOTHER: arrived here at Yale University at 11:30 this morning after a very pleasant trip. You know it was pleasant for me because I had never taken a trip like this before. My only partner and I left Fayetteville Monday night and just arrived at New Haven at 2:00 today, Thursday. But we were furnished Pullman Tickets and were not very fatigued when our journey ended. I want to tell you something about the Red Cross and Y. M. C. A. One never knows very much about these organizations until he gets out away from his home and all his friends. When we left Fayetteville, the canteen service of the Red Cross there gave us wool sweaters, woolen socks and a pair of towels—of course these come in very handy at this latitude, as it is very much cooler here than in Arkansas. We were served at Rogers, Ark. with all kinds of fruit and sandwiches.

Although the government furnished us with meal tickets, we had no need for them until we got to New York and then only because we wished to take in sights, instead of being made comfortable in a Y. M. C. A. building. At Terre Haute, Ind. we were treated very royally. In fact at any station along the road, the ladies are there with their baskets and if soldier, sailor or marine is on board, he gets his fill there and there. We made it convenient to stay overnight in New York although we were not scheduled and we got a bed through Y. M. C. A. for twenty-five cents, which otherwise would have cost 10 or three dollars.
